planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Praecox is an older, full-sized Japanese anemone cultivar whose name reflects its comparatively early bloom window within the Anemone hupehensis group.

directions: Praecox is a standard-height Japanese anemone selection, reaching the typical 3-4 foot bloom height of the group, and is notable chiefly for flowering somewhat earlier in the late-summer-to-fall window than most other Anemone hupehensis cultivars, a trait reflected in its Latin name. It bears the deep rose-pink, single to semi-double flowers with golden centers typical of the species, carried on wiry stems above mounds of coarse, lobed, dark green foliage. It spreads by rhizomes at the normal, fairly vigorous pace of full-sized Japanese anemone selections, so give it room to colonize or plan to divide congested clumps periodically. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, cutting stems back after frost and mulching new plantings their first winter to aid establishment.

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Ernestine Delarue is one of the oldest and most widely grown named croton cultivars, long used for hedging and mixed plantings in South Florida.

directions: Ernestine Delarue is a classic, long-established croton cultivar distinguished by narrow, linear, strap-shaped leaves quite unlike the broad oval blades of large-leaf croton types. Foliage emerges green speckled with yellow and gold and matures to deeper tones of orange, bronze, and red as leaves age, giving established plants a layered, multi-toned effect. It tends to be more tolerant of reduced light than the bold, large-leaved multicolor croton cultivars, though the richest coloring still develops in bright light. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance and drops leaves readily below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.
